explanation: The hypothesis addresses the requested general problem and presents a scientifically plausible, literature-supported alternative: noble-metal-initiated hydrogen spillover across TiO2 can assist low-temperature reduction of base metals and promote homogeneous supported HEA nanoparticles. E1 directly supports this route for TiO2-supported CoNiCuRuPd and its CO2-hydrogenation performance. However, it does not reconstruct the target spray-drying/thermal decomposition-reduction process, unsupported 3D nanoframeworks, 300°C reduction conditions, Pt/Ir/Ru-dependent lattice seeding, Pd failure, Pt–Ru fcc-to-hcp transformation, or methanol oxidation results. Mechanistic agreement is limited to the shared idea that activated hydrogen associated with an initially reduced noble metal facilitates reduction of neighboring base metals. The TiO2-versus-alumina comparison is useful but does not isolate spillover perfectly because support acidity, metal–support interactions, particle size, and precursor dispersion can also differ. A stronger experiment would match particle size and loading and directly measure reduction sequence or migrating hydrogen. The falsification rule should also distinguish failure of the formation mechanism from failure to improve catalytic performance, since a homogeneous alloy need not outperform the control in every reaction.
